title: Build a job description generator
description: A system that turns a rough role brief into a polished, bias-checked job description ready to post.

agent.title: Agent
agent.content: An AI that works independently to complete a goal — planning steps, picking tools, running them, and deciding what to do next without you prompting it at every step. Unlike a chatbot, an agent takes action.

model.title: Model
model.content: A specific trained version of an AI. Claude has several models (like Opus, Sonnet, Haiku) that differ in capability and speed. Larger models are smarter but slower; smaller ones are faster and cheaper.

skill.title: Skill
skill.content: A plain-text file with instructions for a specific repeatable workflow. Save it once, then trigger it with a slash command like /research-competitive. Same steps and output format every time — like a macro for Claude.

slack.title: Slack
slack.content: The team messaging app most companies run on. In Level 2, students connect Slack to their AI tools to trigger workflows from messages, post AI-generated updates to channels, or summarize threads automatically.

claude.title: Claude
claude.content: The AI made by Anthropic. Available as a chat tool at claude.ai, as a desktop app (Claude Desktop), and as a terminal tool (Claude Code). The different interfaces are suited for different types of work.

notion.title: Notion
notion.content: An all-in-one workspace for docs, wikis, databases, and project tracking. Used heavily across the AI Builder program as a destination for AI-generated content and as a connected app in Level 2 automations.

prompt.title: Prompt
prompt.content: The instruction or message you give to an AI. The quality of your prompt directly shapes the quality of the output. Writing better prompts is one of the highest-leverage skills in this program.

rubric.title: Rubric
rubric.content: The written definition of what a good output looks like, in 3–5 scoreable dimensions. Evals grade against a rubric; without one, 'is this good?' is a vibe, not a measurement.

chatgpt.title: ChatGPT
chatgpt.content: OpenAI's chat assistant. The most widely known AI tool — works similarly to Claude but with different strengths and weaknesses. Useful to have access to for cross-checking outputs or trying alternate models.

tool-connectors.title: Tool Connectors
tool-connectors.content: Integrations that let Claude read from and write to apps you use (Gmail, Slack, Google Calendar, Notion, HubSpot, etc.). Set up once in Customize → Connectors. Each connector opens up a new category of tasks Claude can automate.

children.text: Writing job descriptions is the single most common AI use case in recruiting, used by 66% of AI-adopting teams, per [SHRM's Recruiting Executives Priorities and Perspectives 2026](https://www.shrm.org/topics-tools/research/recruiting-executives-priorities-perspectives-2026/repp26-full-report) report. This system takes a rough role brief, a few bullets, a [Slack](#tooltip-slack) message, a past posting, and turns it into a polished, structured draft with a bias check on the wording built in.

Recruiting executives expect generative AI use for job descriptions to keep growing over the next few years, per the same SHRM report. A posting with gendered or exclusionary language narrows the applicant pool before anyone even applies.

Run it as a paste-in [prompt](#tooltip-prompt) every time a requisition opens, a saved skill your team reuses across roles, or a scheduled [agent](#tooltip-agent) that drafts a description the moment a role opens in your tracker.

Open your AI chat and have it interview you into a scope document. Done means a written scope naming where a rough brief usually lands on your desk, the sections your descriptions always need, your company's tone, and the language you want flagged.

children.prompt: I want to build a system with my AI tool that turns a rough role brief into a finished job description. Ask me questions, one at a time, about how a requisition usually reaches me (a hiring manager's notes, a past posting, a Slack thread), what sections my job descriptions always need, what tone or template my company expects, and what language I want it to catch and flag. Then write it up as a scope document I can build from.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: the interview surfaces the sections and tone rules you already follow out of habit, and the scope document becomes the brief for every draft after it.

items: Where the rough brief usually originates, a hiring manager's doc, a Slack thread, or last year's posting.
Whether legal or comp and benefits needs to review before anything gets published.
Whether there's an existing brand template the draft has to match.

children.text: Bring the scope document. Pressure-test it first by pasting it into a fresh session or a different [model](#tooltip-model) and asking it to poke holes. Then gather the [connectors](#tooltip-tool-connectors) it calls for, typically your ATS or job board (Greenhouse, LinkedIn, Indeed), your doc or brand-template source (Google Docs, [Notion](#tooltip-notion), a shared drive folder), and your comp and benefits data if the posting includes a range. The paste-in version needs none.
**Create.** Build and test the system on a real, unedited brief. The prompt below is one example; your scope document has the full version.

children.prompt:
Goal: Turn the rough brief below into a polished job description for [role name] ready to post.

Context: Brief: [paste notes/bullets]. Company voice/template: [link or pasted example]. Level and reporting line: [detail].

Rules:
- Include sections for role summary, responsibilities, must-have and nice-to-have qualifications, and what makes this role different from similar postings elsewhere.
- Flag any word or phrase with known gendered or exclusionary connotations and suggest a neutral replacement.
- Never invent a salary range, benefit, or requirement not present in the brief.
- Output the final posting plus a short "flagged language" list.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: the rule against inventing details keeps the draft honest to the brief, and the flagged-language list makes the bias check visible instead of silent.

children.text: **Review.** Check the output against your scope. Every section present, flagged language reasonable, nothing invented that wasn't in the brief?
**Feedback.** Tell it exactly what went wrong ("this flagged word isn't a problem in our field") and fold each correction into the rules.

items: Build a requisition-to-post pipeline that starts from a hiring manager's raw notes instead of a cleaned-up brief.
Generate tone variants, formal, casual, technical, and let the hiring manager pick.
Turn the language-bias check into a standing rubric the tool applies on every posting.
Pair it with an interview scorecard generator so the posting's must-haves become the scoring rubric automatically.

children.text: **Measure** with a [rubric](#tooltip-rubric). Have your AI chat turn the scope bar into pass/fail checks and a run log in one pass.

children.prompt: From my scope document, write a rubric for judging each job description draft, with 4 to 6 pass/fail checks. Then set up a simple run log I can keep in a doc or spreadsheet, with columns for date, role, flagged terms caught, edits made before posting, and whether legal or comp reviewed it. Give me both in a format I can paste into my notes.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: pass/fail checks remove the judgment call, and the log columns make a drifting tone or a missed flag visible after a few postings.

children.text: **Log** every run. Note the date, which rubric checks passed or failed, and what changed. A single miss is noise, and a repeated miss is an instruction you haven't written yet.

**Make skills** from what the log shows. Once the rubric passes a few postings straight, package the prompt and corrected rules into a skill, so every run starts from your defaults. A repeated failure earns its own skill. [Claude](#tooltip-claude)'s skill-creator skill will interview you and write it, and a custom GPT does the same in [ChatGPT](#tooltip-chatgpt).

One durable failure mode. A generator trained on your past postings will happily repeat whatever bias was already baked into them. Review the flagged-language list yourself before the posting goes live.
